summary: This RFC discusses congestion in a packet switch with infinite storage. Such a switch never runs out of buffers, yet it can still become congested, since delay grows. It asks for discussion of the problem and solutions.

eli5.summary: Even a post office with endless room for mail gets bad if the mail piles up and arrives far too late.

questions: what happens with infinite buffers in packet switches
why does congestion happen even with unlimited storage
why do queues cause packet loss
subtitle: Why unlimited buffers don't solve packet congestion, and how fair queuing helps.

tldr.problem: Packet switching systems can become congested even with infinite buffer storage; the real problem is not running out of memory but excessive delay.
tldr.mechanism: With time-to-live (TTL) limits on packets, extremely long queues cause packets to expire and be discarded before transmission; fair queuing by source address distributes bandwidth equally and creates incentives for well-behaved hosts.
tldr.outcome: This discussion RFC influenced thinking about congestion control, but does not specify a protocol; modern networks use variants of fair queuing and congestion control algorithms like those in TCP.

today: RFC 970 is a discussion document, not a protocol specification. Its ideas influenced congestion control research and practice. Modern routers implement variants of fair queuing (such as weighted fair queuing) and protocols like TCP use congestion avoidance algorithms based on packet loss and delay feedback.

sections.title: The Congestion Paradox
sections.content:
Historically, packet switching engineers focused on buffer management: building switches with enough memory so they would never drop packets due to buffer exhaustion. RFC 970 challenges this assumption by analyzing a theoretical packet switch with infinite storage. The surprising result: such a switch can still become congested and drop all packets.

The mechanism is simple. Internet packets carry a time-to-live (TTL) field that is decremented at each hop and must be positive to be forwarded. When arrival rate exceeds departure rate, queues grow long. Packets wait so long in the queue that their TTL expires before they can be sent. Once TTL reaches zero, the packet is discarded. Under extreme overload with FIFO (first-in-first-out) queuing, even arriving packets with the shortest possible TTL (value 1) are decremented to zero at the next hop and discarded. The result: the network stops delivering any packets.
sections.eli5: Even with infinite storage, if mail piles up too much, letters expire and never get delivered. The problem is not running out of space but wasting time.

sections.title: Fair Queuing Solution
sections.content:
The RFC proposes fair queuing as a solution. Instead of a single FIFO queue per outgoing link, maintain separate queues for each source host. Serve them in round-robin order, taking one packet from each source in turn. This guarantees that each source host gets an equal fraction of the outgoing link's bandwidth, regardless of how many packets it sends.

Fair queuing creates new incentives. Under FIFO, a host gains bandwidth by sending more packets (since it claims more queue slots). Under fair queuing, sending more packets only means packets wait longer in the host's own queue. A host optimizes by sending just enough packets to keep one queued at each switch, minimizing its own transit delay. Badly-behaved hosts that send many packets simply experience longer delays for their own traffic, without blocking well-behaved hosts.

The RFC also proposes using IP's Source Quench mechanism to provide feedback: a switch sends a Source Quench message to a host when that host's queue grows beyond a threshold (e.g., 2 packets), signaling the host to slow down.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big line, give each person their own line and take one person from each line in order. Cheaters can jump in more, but they just get longer waits for themselves, not for honest people.

sections.title: Game Theory and Network Incentives
sections.content:
The RFC frames congestion as a game-theory problem, applying the classic tragedy of the commons analogy. When each participant benefits from using more resources but the shared resource degrades as usage increases, self-interest leads everyone to overuse it and collectively cause collapse. Networks face this: each host benefits from sending more packets, but if all hosts do so, throughput plummets.

Solutions fall into three categories: cooperative (everyone agrees to be nice), authoritarian (rules enforced), and market-based (change the game so selfish behavior is optimal). The RFC argues that fair queuing is a market-based solution: it makes it pay to be well-behaved by ensuring that selfish behavior (sending more packets) harms only the selfish sender, not others.
sections.eli5: Everyone at the commons wants more grazing land, so everyone brings more sheep, and the land dies. Fair queuing makes each person get an equal share no matter how many sheep they bring, so they can't gain by cheating.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Fair queuing's main cost is maintaining separate queues for each source host. The RFC notes this is simpler than it might appear. A practical approach uses singly-linked per-host queues, with doubly-linked queue heads to allow efficient deletion of empty queues. Only three pointers per buffer are needed. When buffers are exhausted, drop the packet at the end of the longest queue (the one from the heaviest sender), which is both fair and discourages aggressive senders.

The RFC emphasizes that the overhead is modest and the complexity is not greater than other data structure approaches like balanced binary trees. This made fair queuing practical to implement in real packet switches, and variants of it have become common in modern routers and end-host systems.
sections.eli5: To keep separate lines, you just need to link each packet to the next one in its line. When you run out of space, drop from the longest line, which is fair.
